intro.title:
Payment system
Stripe / PayPal-style
intro.subtitle: Twelve transactions per second is easy. Never charging twice, never losing a cent and proving it in an audit is the design.

cues.cap: Designing a payment system and digital wallet, scenario by scenario.

The volume is small: 12 transactions per second, 120 at peak. The hard part is correctness: idempotency at every hop, double-entry bookkeeping instead of a balance column, and accepting that exactly-once does not exist.
cues.say: The volume is small: twelve transactions per second, a hundred and twenty at peak. The hard part is correctness: idempotency at every hop, double-entry bookkeeping instead of a balance column, and accepting that exactly-once does not exist.

scenes.title: Seven services around one principle: idempotency

steps.cap: The synchronous path: the client calls our API with an Idempotency-Key, Payment Service checks Redis, asks Risk Service for the hard rules and calls the PSP with the same key. Card data goes straight from the browser to Stripe and never touches us.
steps.say: The synchronous path: the client calls our A P I with an idempotency key, Payment Service checks Redis, asks Risk Service for the hard rules and calls the P S P with the same key. Card data goes straight from the browser to Stripe and never touches us.
steps.title: Sync payment path
steps.note: The sync answer is only 202 accepted. The final state of a payment always comes from a webhook.

steps.cap: The asynchronous path: signed webhooks from the PSP change the payment state, events leave through the outbox into Kafka, and every money movement becomes a double-entry transfer in Ledger Service.
steps.say: The asynchronous path: signed webhooks from the P S P change the payment state, events leave through the outbox into Kafka, and every money movement becomes a double-entry transfer in Ledger Service.
steps.title: Async path
steps.note: Ledger Service is separate because money is recorded as balanced entries, never as a balance column that gets updated.

steps.cap: And every night Reconciliation Job compares our ledger with the PSP's settlement file; mismatches go to the Ops Dashboard.
steps.say: And every night Reconciliation Job compares our ledger with the P S P's settlement file; mismatches go to the Ops Dashboard.
steps.title: Reconciliation
steps.note: The system is designed on the assumption that mismatches will happen; the question is how fast they are caught.

steps.cap: The customer clicks Pay 100 EUR. The browser calls POST /payments with amount, currency and an Idempotency-Key, a UUID generated on the client; the gateway authenticates and forwards it over gRPC.
steps.say: The customer clicks Pay one hundred euros. The browser calls post slash payments with amount, currency and an idempotency key, a U U I D generated on the client; the gateway authenticates and forwards it over G R P C.
steps.code:
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 9c1e…f4
{ amount: 10000, currency: 'EUR', merchant: 'm7' }
→ gRPC Payments.Create(...)
steps.note: Amounts are integers in minor units: 10000 is 100.00 EUR. Never floats.

steps.cap: Payment Service does SET NX on the key in Redis with a 24-hour TTL. The key is new, so it continues. A UNIQUE constraint on the key in Postgres is the second line of defence.
steps.say: Payment Service does set N X on the key in Redis with a twenty-four hour T T L. The key is new, so it continues. A unique constraint on the key in Postgres is the second line of defence.
steps.code:
SET idem:9c1e…f4 pay_51 NX EX 86400
→ OK   (new request)

steps.cap: It inserts a payments row in state CREATED and returns a client_secret to the browser.
steps.say: It inserts a payments row in state created and returns a client secret to the browser.

steps.cap: The browser hands the card to Stripe's iframe directly. Card numbers never pass through our servers, so the PCI audit is theirs, not ours. Stripe returns a token.
steps.say: The browser hands the card to Stripe's iframe directly. Card numbers never pass through our servers, so the P C I audit is theirs, not ours. Stripe returns a token.
steps.code:
Stripe.js → tokenize(card, cvc, exp)
← tok_visa_4242     (never seen by us)
3DS challenge if the issuer asks

steps.cap: Payment Service calls Risk Service over gRPC with a 50-millisecond deadline for the hard rules: block lists, five cards from one account in a minute, card country versus IP. ML scoring runs later, asynchronously.
steps.say: Payment Service calls Risk Service over G R P C with a fifty millisecond deadline for the hard rules: block lists, five cards from one account in a minute, card country versus I P. M L scoring runs later, asynchronously.
steps.code:
gRPC Risk.Check(user, card_bin, ip, amount)
deadline: 50 ms
← { decision: 'allow', score: 0.12 }

ML scoring: Kafka consumer, may hold capture

steps.cap: Then it calls Stripe over HTTPS for authorize plus capture with the same Idempotency-Key. If our request is repeated, Stripe returns the old response instead of a second charge. Stripe answers pending.
steps.say: Then it calls Stripe over H T T P S for authorize plus capture with the same idempotency key. If our request is repeated, Stripe returns the old response instead of a second charge. Stripe answers pending.
steps.code:
POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/payment_intents
Idempotency-Key: 9c1e…f4
amount=10000 currency=eur capture=automatic
← 200 { id: 'pi_7a', status: 'processing' }

steps.cap: We return 202 with the payment id. The final status does not come from this response; it comes from a webhook seconds later.
steps.say: We return two-oh-two with the payment I D. The final status does not come from this response; it comes from a webhook seconds later.
steps.title: Payment Service → Client
steps.code:
HTTP 202 Accepted
{ payment_id: 'pay_51', state: 'PROCESSING' }

steps.cap: Stripe sends the webhook payment.captured. Webhook Handler verifies the HMAC signature, stores the event with INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and answers 200 immediately. Processing happens after the 200.
steps.say: Stripe sends the webhook payment captured. Webhook Handler verifies the H mac signature, stores the event with insert on conflict do nothing, and answers two hundred immediately. Processing happens after the two hundred.
steps.code:
POST /webhooks/stripe
Stripe-Signature: t=…,v1=…   ✓ verified
{ id: 'evt_e9', type: 'payment.captured', pay_51 }
INSERT INTO payment_events (id) VALUES ('evt_e9')
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;   → 200

steps.cap: Then a conditional UPDATE moves the payment to CAPTURED only from CREATED or AUTHORIZED. One row affected means the transition is ours to act on.
steps.say: Then a conditional update moves the payment to captured only from created or authorized. One row affected means the transition is ours to act on.
steps.code:
UPDATE payments SET state = 'CAPTURED'
 WHERE id = 'pay_51'
   AND state IN ('CREATED', 'AUTHORIZED');
→ 1 row affected
steps.note: No SELECT before the UPDATE, no distributed lock: the row count is the answer.

steps.cap: It calls Ledger Service: one transfer of three entries, customer minus 10 000, merchant plus 9 710, fees plus 290. The sum is zero and the rows are append-only, never updated.
steps.say: It calls Ledger Service: one transfer of three entries, customer minus ten thousand, merchant plus nine thousand seven hundred and ten, fees plus two hundred and ninety. The sum is zero and the rows are append-only, never updated.
steps.code:
gRPC Ledger.Transfer(ref: 'pay_51'):
  customer:u42    -10000
  merchant:m7      +9710
  fees:platform     +290     sum = 0
INSERT INTO ledger_entries ... (no UPDATE, no DELETE)
steps.note: A balance is a report over entries, not a column. The audit trail is the data itself.

steps.cap: The state change leaves through the outbox into Kafka payment-events. Workers consume it: receipt email, analytics, and batched payouts to the merchant through the PSP.
steps.say: The state change leaves through the outbox into Kafka payment events. Workers consume it: receipt email, analytics, and batched payouts to the merchant through the P S P.
steps.code:
outbox → produce payment-events
  { payment: 'pay_51', state: 'CAPTURED' }
consumers: email receipt · analytics · payouts
→ gRPC Ledger.Transfer for payouts

scenes.title: A lost response and a duplicated webhook

steps.cap: The network drops right after we returned 202 and the browser never sees it. The user clicks Pay again. The same Idempotency-Key arrives, and SET NX says the key already exists.
steps.say: The network drops right after we returned two-oh-two and the browser never sees it. The user clicks Pay again. The same idempotency key arrives, and set N X says the key already exists.
steps.title: Same request again
steps.code:
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 9c1e…f4   (same)
SET idem:9c1e…f4 pay_51 NX EX 86400
→ (nil)   key exists

steps.cap: Payment Service returns the same payment_id and the same response: no new row, no second charge. If Redis lost the key in a failover, the UNIQUE constraint in Postgres catches it. The same key with a different amount is a 422, a client error, not a second payment.
steps.say: Payment Service returns the same payment I D and the same response: no new row, no second charge. If Redis lost the key in a failover, the unique constraint in Postgres catches it. The same key with a different amount is a four twenty-two, a client error, not a second payment.
steps.title: Same key → same response
steps.code:
→ 202 { payment_id: 'pay_51' }   (stored response)

UNIQUE (idempotency_key)  → second defence
same key, different amount → 422 Unprocessable

steps.cap: Later Stripe delivers the same webhook evt_e9 a second time; they resend by design, at-least-once. INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING inserts nothing, processing stops, and the ledger never gets a second transfer.
steps.say: Later Stripe delivers the same webhook a second time; they resend by design, at least once. Insert on conflict do nothing inserts nothing, processing stops, and the ledger never gets a second transfer.
steps.title: Duplicate webhook
steps.code:
POST /webhooks/stripe  { id: 'evt_e9', ... }  (again)
INSERT INTO payment_events (id) VALUES ('evt_e9')
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;  → 0 rows
→ 200, nothing else happens

steps.cap: Webhooks also arrive out of order. captured before authorized is accepted, because the PSP knows more than we do; the late authorized on a CAPTURED row affects zero rows and changes nothing.
steps.say: Webhooks also arrive out of order. Captured before authorized is accepted, because the P S P knows more than we do; the late authorized on a captured row affects zero rows and changes nothing.
steps.title: Out-of-order webhooks

steps.cap: Idempotency on every hop: client to us by Idempotency-Key, us to the PSP by the same key, and the PSP to us by webhook event id.
steps.say: Idempotency on every hop: client to us by idempotency key, us to the P S P by the same key, and the P S P to us by webhook event I D.
steps.title: Three hops, three keys
steps.code:
client → us:   Idempotency-Key  (Redis + UNIQUE)
us → PSP:      Idempotency-Key  (same)
PSP → us:      event_id         (ON CONFLICT)

steps.cap: At 03:00 Reconciliation Job downloads yesterday's settlement file from Stripe: a CSV with every movement and every fee.
steps.say: At three in the morning Reconciliation Job downloads yesterday's settlement file from Stripe: a C S V with every movement and every fee.
steps.code:
GET /v1/reporting/report_runs/…/download
→ settlement_2026-10-12.csv   184 312 rows

steps.cap: It compares the file row by row with ledger_entries, matching on the PSP charge id, amount and fee.
steps.say: It compares the file row by row with ledger entries, matching on the P S P charge I D, amount and fee.
steps.code:
SELECT psp_charge_id, amount, fee
  FROM ledger_entries
 WHERE booked_at::date = '2026-10-12';
match ⟷ settlement rows

steps.cap: Three kinds of mismatch. A payment at Stripe we have no record of: a lost webhook that retries never delivered; we create the record and alarm. A payment we marked paid with no money at Stripe: an incident. A different amount or fee: a correcting reversing entry, never an UPDATE.
steps.say: Three kinds of mismatch. A payment at Stripe we have no record of: a lost webhook that retries never delivered; we create the record and alarm. A payment we marked paid with no money at Stripe: an incident. A different amount or fee: a correcting reversing entry, never an update.
steps.title: Three kinds of mismatch
steps.code:
psp only   → create record + alarm
ours only  → incident (paid, no money)
amount ≠   → reversing entry (append, no UPDATE)

day poller: CREATED > 15 min → GET /payments/:id

steps.cap: The night ends with a zero-mismatch report or a list for manual intervention in the Ops Dashboard. The system assumes mismatches will happen; the question is how fast they are caught.
steps.code:
report 2026-10-12:
  184 309 matched · 3 mismatches
→ Ops Dashboard queue, with the raw rows

steps.cap: The same job computes payouts: each merchant's balance minus a rolling reserve for chargebacks, paid in batches with the idempotent key merchant_id plus period, so a restart never pays twice.
steps.say: The same job computes payouts: each merchant's balance minus a rolling reserve for chargebacks, paid in batches with the idempotent key merchant I D plus period, so a restart never pays twice.
steps.title: Payouts, once
steps.code:
payout m7 / 2026-10-12:
  balance 9710 − reserve 10 % = 8739
  Idempotency-Key: 'm7:2026-10-12'
POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/payouts

recap.title: What to say in the interview

items.text: Idempotency on three hops: client → us → PSP → webhook
items.cap: To sum up. Idempotency on every hop: a client key, the same key to the PSP, and the event id on the webhook.
items.say: To sum up. Idempotency on every hop: a client key, the same key to the P S P, and the event I D on the webhook.

items.text: Card data never touches us: tokenize at the PSP
items.cap: Card data never touches our servers; the PSP tokenizes it and owns the PCI scope.
items.say: Card data never touches our servers; the P S P tokenizes it and owns the P C I scope.

items.text: State machine with conditional UPDATEs; webhooks are the truth
items.cap: Payment state moves only through conditional UPDATEs, driven by signed, deduplicated webhooks.
items.say: Payment state moves only through conditional updates, driven by signed, deduplicated webhooks.

items.text: Double-entry ledger: append-only, sum = 0, balance is a report
items.cap: Money is a double-entry ledger: append-only entries that sum to zero. A balance is a report, not a column.

items.text: Nightly reconciliation against the settlement file
items.cap: And a nightly reconciliation against the settlement file, because mismatches will happen. Exactly-once does not exist; idempotency does.
